question: Your dashboard makes fifty database calls per page load. How would you find and remove unnecessary requests?
key_points: Trace the calls to identify repeated lookups, per-item queries and genuinely separate work | Batch related lookups or fetch related data together when the query shape supports it | Deduplicate repeated requests within a page load before adding cross-request caching | Cache only data with a defined key, freshness policy and authorization scope | Compare query counts, returned data volume and end-to-end latency before and after the change
common_misconceptions: Running every query in parallel reduces the number of database requests | A single huge join is always better than several targeted queries | Caching all responses is safe regardless of user identity
probes: What evidence would reveal an N-plus-one query pattern? | When could a batch or join fetch too much data?

twist_key_points: Coalesce the repeated lookup or reuse its result within the request | Do not treat identical lookups as forty-nine distinct relationships needing a large join | Add broader caching only if reuse across requests and acceptable freshness justify it

question: How is batching database requests different from simply running them in parallel?
key_points: Batching combines compatible work into fewer round trips | Parallel execution can overlap latency while leaving the number of database operations unchanged | Unbounded parallelism can overload connections, CPU or storage | Batch size, error handling and returned data volume must remain manageable | Choose an approach using the query pattern and measured database bottleneck
common_misconceptions: Parallel requests are the same as a batched query | The largest possible batch always has the lowest latency | A connection pool creates unlimited database capacity
probes: What could make a batch slower than smaller requests? | How would you limit concurrency without losing all latency benefit?
twist: Now the calls target separate services that offer no batch interface. How does your approach change?
twist_key_points: Use bounded concurrency rather than assuming the work can be merged into one query | Consider an aggregation endpoint or request-level reuse only where the service contracts allow it | Measure downstream load and timeouts as well as page latency

question: Many pages repeatedly fetch the same rarely changing category list. What would you consider before adding a cache?
key_points: Measure how often the list is reused and how expensive the lookup actually is | Define the cache key including any locale, tenant or permission differences | Choose a freshness and update policy that matches how the list changes | Set memory bounds and decide what happens on cache failure or a miss | Measure hit rate and database load rather than assuming the cache helps
common_misconceptions: Rarely changing data never needs invalidation | A cache key can ignore tenant or locale differences | A cache failure should trigger unlimited concurrent database lookups
probes: Would you cache the list in the process or in shared storage? | What would tell you the cache is adding complexity without useful benefit?
twist: Now the category list differs for every tenant and includes confidential labels. What changes?
twist_key_points: Scope keys and access checks to the correct tenant | Prevent one tenant from receiving cached data belonging to another | Reassess whether per-tenant reuse justifies the memory and invalidation complexity

question: How would you choose a time-to-live for cached data?
key_points: Start with the business tolerance for stale values rather than a convenient default | Consider update frequency, access pattern and origin cost | A longer lifetime can improve reuse but prolong an incorrect value | Combine expiry with invalidation or version checks when freshness requirements need them | Plan expiry behavior, refresh concurrency and a safe failure policy
common_misconceptions: A cached value is guaranteed current until its expiry time | A longer time-to-live is always better | Expiry alone can guarantee immediate visibility of every update
probes: Would you use the same lifetime for a public description and a permission check? | What happens when many popular keys expire together?
twist: Now a displayed price must match the authoritative price used at checkout. What changes?
twist_key_points: A time-to-live alone cannot guarantee that equality | Validate the authoritative price or an explicit price version at the pricing decision | If the earlier displayed quote must be honored, persist a versioned quote with a clear validity policy

question: A user updates a product, but other sessions still see the old cached value. How would you make updates appear reliably?
key_points: Identify the database source of truth and every writer of the product | Order cache changes relative to a successful database commit | Account for stale refill races rather than assuming deletion alone prevents old values returning | Use versioned values or reliable change notifications where needed, with recovery for missed updates | Define read-your-writes behavior and use expiry only within the acceptable freshness limit | Test concurrent reads, failed writes and delayed invalidation
common_misconceptions: Deleting a cache key before a database commit guarantees freshness | A cache update and database update are automatically atomic | A long expiry is an adequate substitute for strict freshness
probes: How could an old read refill the cache after invalidation? | What should happen if the database commit succeeds but notification delivery fails? | How would you let the updating user read the new value immediately?
twist: Now updates also come from a bulk-import process that never calls the application. What changes?
twist_key_points: Application-only invalidation no longer covers every writer | Use a database change feed, coordinated import notifications or another mechanism that observes those commits | Recheck versioning, recovery and freshness guarantees across all update paths

question: When would you add a database index, and what might it cost?
key_points: Start from frequent or slow query filters, joins and ordering requirements | Check the execution plan and how many rows the query is expected to match | An appropriate index can reduce lookup or ordering work but is not always chosen | Indexes consume storage and add work to inserts, updates and deletes | Measure benefits on representative reads and writes and avoid redundant indexes
common_misconceptions: Every indexed query becomes constant-time | An index is always faster than scanning a table | Adding indexes has no effect on write cost or storage
probes: Why might a database ignore an available index? | How would you decide whether two similar indexes are both worth keeping?
twist: Now the table is tiny and almost every query reads all rows. What changes?
twist_key_points: A scan may already be inexpensive and preferable | Do not add an index without a demonstrated query benefit | Balance the small possible read improvement against maintenance and complexity

question: An activity feed filters by account and sorts by creation time, but slows as data grows. How would you investigate indexing?
key_points: Inspect the actual query plan, filter values and returned row counts | Test an index whose leading fields match the account filter and required ordering | Include a stable tie-breaker when creation timestamps are not unique | Check whether the query needs extra table reads or fetches unnecessary columns | Measure write overhead and plan an index build that respects production load
common_misconceptions: Separate indexes on every field always equal one suitable composite index | An index guarantees a stable order when timestamps tie | An index can fix unnecessary application queries by itself
probes: Why does the order of fields in a composite index matter? | What would you measure before and after adding it?
twist: Now most queries filter only by creation time across every account. What changes?
twist_key_points: The old account-leading index may be less useful for the new access pattern | Test a time-leading index and inspect the resulting plans | Reassess whether to keep both indexes using the actual read and write workload

question: After saving a change, a user sometimes reads the old value from a read replica. How would you handle that?
key_points: Recognize that an asynchronous replica can lag the committed primary | Decide whether this operation requires read-your-writes behavior | Route the relevant follow-up read to an authoritative source or wait for the required replication progress | Do not assume a fixed sleep always covers replication delay | Monitor lag and define what happens when the freshness requirement cannot be met
common_misconceptions: A successful write means every replica already has it | Read replicas automatically increase write throughput | Adding more replicas removes replication lag
probes: Which reads could still safely use a replica? | How would you avoid routing every read to the primary forever?
twist: Now the primary is unavailable and no reachable replica is known to contain that update. What changes?
twist_key_points: Do not promise a fresh value that the reachable replicas cannot establish | Return a documented pending or unavailable outcome if freshness is required | Serve an explicitly stale value only if the operation permits that behavior

question: What is the difference between adding read replicas and sharding a database?
key_points: Read replicas copy a dataset and can offload suitable reads | Sharding distributes different portions of the logical data across database nodes | A shard key should match access patterns and avoid severe load or storage skew | Cross-shard queries, transactions and rebalancing add coordination work | Measure the actual bottleneck and consider simpler query or indexing improvements first
common_misconceptions: A replica stores a different partition by definition | Sharding automatically speeds every query by the number of shards | Partitioning tables inside one server necessarily adds independent server capacity
probes: What makes a poor shard key? | Why can a cross-customer report become harder after sharding?
twist: Now the only bottleneck is repeated reads, rather than storage or writes. What would you prioritize?
twist_key_points: Evaluate query improvements, caching and suitable read replicas before repartitioning data | Keep replica freshness requirements explicit | Do not take on cross-shard complexity solely to solve a read pattern a simpler option can handle

question: A fixed-window rate limit permits a sharp burst around the minute boundary. How would you change the design?
key_points: Define whether the goal is a strict rolling limit, a long-run rate or a controlled burst | Recognize that requests can cluster on opposite sides of a fixed reset | Compare a rolling-window approach with a token bucket using the required semantics | Apply limits atomically for the chosen identity across relevant server instances | Return a clear throttled response and retry guidance while keeping the limiter itself bounded
common_misconceptions: A token bucket automatically enforces any strict rolling-window contract | Independent per-server counters enforce one global limit | Rate limiting and unlimited request queuing are equivalent
probes: What burst would a token bucket intentionally allow? | How would you decide whether an approximate sliding counter is acceptable?
twist: Now the contract forbids more than one hundred requests in any rolling sixty-second interval. What changes?
twist_key_points: Use an exact rolling-window admission rule or another implementation with a proven conservative bound | Do not assume a token bucket with burst capacity meets this stricter contract | Coordinate updates atomically and define the interval boundary convention

question: A per-IP rate limit blocks many legitimate users on a shared network. How would you make the policy fairer?
key_points: Use authenticated user or application identity when available rather than relying only on IP addresses | Keep a bounded anonymous policy for clients without a trusted identity | Combine per-principal protection with service-wide and expensive-operation limits | Account for shared networks without trusting a client-supplied identity header blindly | Monitor blocked legitimate traffic and abuse before tuning thresholds
common_misconceptions: One IP address always identifies one person | Any identity header supplied by the client is trustworthy | Removing every limit is the only way to avoid unfair blocking
probes: How would you treat a user who owns many accounts? | Which measurements would reveal that the policy is hurting legitimate users?
twist: Now the endpoint is public and requests have no authenticated identity. What changes?
twist_key_points: Use layered anonymous controls such as network, validated session and operation-level limits | Do not substitute an easily forged identity for authentication | Keep global capacity protection and assess false positives for shared networks

question: Generating a large report exceeds the request timeout. How would you redesign the flow?
key_points: Accept the work through a durable job mechanism rather than holding a request open indefinitely | Return a job reference and a clear pending status | Let bounded workers process the job and expose completion or failure | Make repeated submissions and worker retries safe under the application contract | Define access control, result retention, cancellation and a realistic completion expectation
common_misconceptions: A queue makes report generation instantaneous | Acknowledging a request proves the report has completed | Retrying a job can never duplicate its side effects
probes: How would the client find out that the report failed? | What would stop one user from filling the entire queue?
twist: Now the report must represent one transactionally consistent snapshot of changing records. What changes?

question: What can a queue improve during a traffic burst, and what problems does it leave unsolved?
key_points: A queue can separate request arrival from the time workers perform the work | Durable buffering can absorb a temporary mismatch between arrival and processing rates | A queue does not create processing capacity or fix sustained overload | Backlog size and age affect user waiting time and resource use | Bound the queue and define admission, retries, failure handling and recovery
common_misconceptions: A larger queue permanently solves a worker-capacity shortage | Durable delivery implies each business effect occurs exactly once | Queue length alone tells you whether the oldest job meets its deadline
probes: Why could backlog keep rising even while workers are busy? | When should you reject or defer new work rather than keep accepting it?
twist: Now every request must return a completed result within half a second. What changes?
twist_key_points: Include queue wait in the end-to-end latency budget | Use bounded admission and enough immediate capacity rather than relying on delayed asynchronous completion | Consider caching or precomputation where valid, and fail clearly when the completion promise cannot be met

question: Clients retry after a timeout and sometimes create duplicate orders. How would you make order creation safe to retry?
key_points: Treat a timeout as an unknown outcome rather than proof that nothing happened | Use a stable operation key scoped to the caller and the same logical request | Atomically prevent competing attempts from creating multiple orders | Persist the operation state or result consistently with the business write | Check that key reuse has the same request contents and define retention and pending behavior | Return the original outcome for a valid duplicate rather than repeat its business effect
common_misconceptions: A retry must use a fresh idempotency key | Checking a cache before an insert prevents all concurrent duplicates | A local deduplication record automatically controls every external side effect
probes: What if the first request commits but its response is lost? | What if two attempts arrive at the same time?
twist: Now simultaneous requests reuse one key with different order contents. What changes?
twist_key_points: Reject mismatched key reuse with a documented conflict or validation outcome | Compare the request identity or contents atomically with the stored operation | Do not create both orders or return an unrelated successful result as though the requests matched

question: When is it safe for a client to retry an API request after a timeout?
key_points: The original request may have taken effect despite the lost response | Safety depends on the intended repeated effect, not merely receiving the same response code | Use a defined idempotent operation or a supported stable operation key when repeating a write | Retry transient failures with bounded attempts, deadlines and backoff rather than every error | Coordinate retries across layers and respect applicable service retry guidance
common_misconceptions: A timeout proves the server did not perform the action | Every request becomes safe to retry if the delay is long enough | Idempotency means every repeated response must be byte-for-byte identical
probes: Why can retrying at several layers amplify load? | How would you handle a request whose outcome remains unknown?
twist: Now the operation sends a message through a provider that cannot deduplicate or reveal delivery status. What changes?
twist_key_points: A local retry policy cannot guarantee exactly one external delivery in this situation | Choose the acceptable duplicate-versus-missed-delivery policy and a reconciliation path explicitly | Do not blindly repeat an uncertain send while claiming that the local operation key removes all risk

question: A paginated feed sometimes repeats or skips items while new records arrive. How would you investigate and improve it?
key_points: Check whether offset positions are shifting as records are inserted or removed | Define a deterministic order with a unique tie-breaker | Consider keyset pagination using the last ordering values rather than only a row offset | Keep filters and authorization consistent across pages | Decide whether the feed is live or must preserve a snapshot; a cursor alone does not freeze changing data
common_misconceptions: Sorting only by a nonunique timestamp guarantees stable pages | A cursor automatically creates a database snapshot | Large offsets are always free because only one page is returned
probes: What belongs in a cursor when timestamps can tie? | How should a filter change affect an existing cursor?
twist: Now users require direct jumps to arbitrary numbered pages. What changes?
twist_key_points: Keyset traversal alone does not provide arbitrary page-number lookup | Consider an indexed page map, retained snapshot or offset approach depending on scale and freshness | Keep the existing consistency requirements explicit rather than solving navigation by silently changing the feed contract

question: How would you choose between offset pagination and cursor pagination?
key_points: Offset pagination is simple and supports page-number navigation | Large offsets can require substantial skipped-row work depending on the database plan | Cursor or keyset pagination can continue from an indexed ordering position | Use a deterministic order and a unique tie-breaker for either approach | Consider changing data, snapshot needs, token validation and user navigation requirements
common_misconceptions: Cursor pagination is always the right choice for every dataset | An opaque cursor removes the need for authorization checks | Offset pagination necessarily produces incorrect results on immutable data
probes: Why might a cursor need to include filter information? | When is the simplicity of offsets worth keeping?
twist: Now the result is a small immutable report navigated by page number. What changes?
twist_key_points: A simple offset approach may fit the bounded size and navigation requirement well | Immutability removes the shifting-position issue for this report | Measure performance before adding cursor or snapshot infrastructure that the use case does not need

question: How would you design a simple API for creating, reading and updating orders as resources?
key_points: Use an order collection and stable identifiers for individual orders | Use retrieval methods without intended write effects and creation or update methods with defined semantics | Distinguish full replacement from partial update where the interface supports both | Specify validation, errors and response representations as part of the contract | Authorize access to each resource rather than trusting its identifier | Document retry behavior and compatibility instead of relying on route names alone
common_misconceptions: A read method is safe to use for changing orders if it returns success | Knowing an order identifier proves the caller may access it | Every business operation must be forced into an identical create-or-update shape
probes: How would a client distinguish creating a new order from updating an existing one? | What would you document about invalid input and missing resources?
twist: Now clients choose stable order identifiers and must safely repeat creation after a lost response. What changes?
twist_key_points: Consider an idempotent create-or-replace contract at the known resource identity, such as a suitable PUT design | Define behavior for an existing identifier with different contents rather than creating another order | Keep identifier ownership and authorization checks in the contract

question: Your API accepts a report request but finishes it later. What should the immediate response tell the client?
key_points: Clearly distinguish accepted work from a completed report | An accepted-processing response such as 202 can communicate that the work is not finished | Return a job reference and a way to observe completion or failure | A created job resource can justify 201 under that resource contract without claiming the report is complete | Document status transitions, authorization and how long the client should retain or poll the reference
common_misconceptions: An accepted response proves processing will eventually succeed | The status code alone communicates all job progress | The client must keep the original connection open until every background task finishes
probes: What should a client do if the job later fails? | How would you prevent aggressive polling from becoming a new bottleneck?
twist: Now the report is fully generated before the response is sent. What changes?
twist_key_points: Return a completed result rather than only promising future processing | Choose success semantics for the actual contract, such as returning a representation or identifying a newly created report | Keep background-job machinery only if it serves another explicit requirement

question: You need to rename a response field, but older clients still rely on it. How would you evolve the API?
key_points: Treat removal or changed meaning as a compatibility concern for existing consumers | Consider an additive transition that exposes the new field while retaining the old contract | Use a documented versioning and deprecation policy when a breaking change is necessary | Measure usage and communicate migration rather than assuming clients deploy together | Test both old and new contracts and define a deliberate end to support
common_misconceptions: Changing a field name is always a harmless internal refactor | Adding a version number removes the need to support existing clients | All clients can be upgraded at the same moment
probes: How would you know whether the old field is still used? | What would make an additive transition misleading or unsafe?
twist: Now the old field exposes sensitive data and must stop being returned immediately. What changes?
twist_key_points: Prioritize removing the data exposure over a normal long deprecation period | Communicate the emergency behavior change and provide a safe replacement where possible | Monitor client failures without restoring the unsafe field as a routine rollback

question: What does choosing consistency over availability mean when two groups of replicas cannot communicate?
key_points: State that the trade-off applies during the communication partition | For a linearizable operation, replicas must behave like one up-to-date copy rather than independently confirm conflicting results | A node may need to refuse or delay operations it cannot safely coordinate | Availability in this context is not simply the same as an uptime percentage | Choose behavior for the business operation rather than declaring one policy best for every kind of data
common_misconceptions: Consistency and availability can never coexist even without a partition | Serving any cached response proves strict consistency | The same choice is required for an optional counter and an inventory reservation
probes: What would a caller observe when a write cannot be safely accepted? | Why can returning an old value be unacceptable for some operations? | Which product requirement determines whether stale reads are tolerable?
twist: Now the data is an optional public popularity counter and approximate values are acceptable. What changes?
twist_key_points: Serving approximate values or accepting suitably reconcilable updates during the partition may be acceptable | Define how concurrent increments are merged without silently losing counts | Do not extend that relaxed policy automatically to unrelated operations requiring stronger guarantees

question: Two regions show one remaining item, and both can accept purchases. How would you prevent selling the same item twice?
key_points: Do not treat a stale display as authority to commit an inventory sale | Use an atomic reservation or conditional stock update under a defined authoritative coordination model | Route or coordinate competing purchases so only one valid reservation succeeds | Use idempotency for repeated attempts while recognizing that distinct buyers are a separate race | Define an explicit failure or pending behavior when safe coordination is unavailable
common_misconceptions: A cache invalidation message alone prevents every concurrent oversell | An idempotency key automatically coordinates two different buyers | Reading the stock and later writing a lower value is always atomic
probes: What happens if the buyer retries after the reservation succeeds? | What should a disconnected region do if it cannot confirm stock authority?
twist: Now the product is a downloadable file with unlimited copies. What changes?
twist_key_points: Remove the unnecessary single-unit stock reservation constraint | Independent purchases need not coordinate around scarce inventory | Still enforce payment or order deduplication, authorization and delivery rules where applicable

question: What does a load balancer do, and what does it not solve?
key_points: Route eligible traffic across healthy serving instances under a defined policy | Use readiness and health checks that reflect whether an instance can serve useful work | Recognize that connection counts, request counts and actual processing load differ | Shared database or external-service bottlenecks can remain after adding application instances | Plan connection draining, timeouts and state handling rather than assuming any request can move anywhere
common_misconceptions: A load balancer creates unlimited capacity in a shared database | Round-robin routing guarantees equal CPU load | An instance is ready for traffic merely because its process exists
probes: Why might a shallow health check miss a real outage? | What should happen to requests already running during a deployment?
twist: Now each request keeps a connection open for an hour. What changes?
twist_key_points: Account for active connection duration and the limits of per-connection routing | New instances may receive new connections without redistributing old ones automatically | Use a deliberate draining or reconnection policy rather than cutting long-running work unexpectedly

question: Your app has several servers, but one receives most requests. What would you investigate before adding more servers?
key_points: Measure distribution and resource use by instance rather than infer imbalance from one symptom | Check session affinity, connection reuse and the routing algorithm | Look for unevenly expensive requests or a few very busy clients | Verify health checks and whether all intended instances are eligible | Check whether local state or a shared bottleneck limits the routing options
common_misconceptions: Every imbalance proves that more servers are needed | Equal request counts always imply equal resource use | A new instance automatically receives part of every existing connection
probes: Could one long-lived client connection explain the pattern? | What would tell you that the database, rather than routing, is the real bottleneck?
twist: Now each request depends on user-session data stored only on one server. What changes?
twist_key_points: Routing freely to another server can now break session correctness | Consider deliberate affinity as a short-term constraint or move session state to a suitable shared or client-carried design | Reassess failover, authorization and session expiry rather than optimizing distribution alone

question: When would you put content behind a CDN, and what would you avoid caching by default?
key_points: Public reusable static content is a strong starting candidate | Nearby cached copies can reduce origin traffic and delivery latency | Define freshness, cache keys and variant handling explicitly | Keep personal or authorization-dependent responses out of shared caching unless a carefully controlled policy supports them | Plan cache misses, origin failure and invalidation rather than treating the CDN as the source of truth

twist_key_points: Default to a policy that prevents unsafe shared reuse | Distinguish private caching, revalidation and no-store requirements according to the data contract | Verify authorization and existing cached copies instead of assuming a URL alone separates users

question: After deployment, some users receive old scripts and a broken page. How would you make static asset updates reliable?
key_points: Use content-versioned asset names when possible so changed bytes have a new identity | Keep page or manifest freshness consistent with how it references the assets | Upload required assets before exposing pages that reference them | Retain older assets long enough for existing pages and rollback needs | Use deliberate invalidation or validation policies rather than depending on every client clearing its cache

probes: Why might a fresh page still break after a correct script upload? | How would you roll back without leaving clients with missing asset versions?

twist_key_points: Do not rely only on renaming the asset | Use an explicit bounded freshness, validation and purge policy for the stable URL | Keep content changes compatible with consumers that may still hold the previous version

question: How do logs, metrics and traces complement each other when investigating a production problem?
key_points: Metrics summarize rates, errors, latency and resource trends for monitoring and alerting | Structured logs describe selected events with useful diagnostic context | Traces connect work across a request path and its dependencies | Use correlation identifiers in appropriate logs and traces while keeping metric labels bounded | Choose sampling, access control and retention policies that protect sensitive data and control cost

question: A popular cached item expires and many requests hit the database together. How would you prevent this surge?
key_points: Coalesce concurrent refreshes for the same key within a defined coordination scope | Consider early refresh or prewarming for predictable hot data | Use expiry jitter to reduce synchronized expiry across keys or cache instances | Serve a previous value during refresh only if the freshness contract permits it | Bound origin concurrency and define a safe fallback when refresh fails
common_misconceptions: Adding more application servers necessarily reduces total origin work | Expiry jitter alone guarantees one refresh for a single shared key | Serving stale data is acceptable for every kind of value

twist_key_points: Do not use a stale authorization value merely to preserve availability | Use an authoritative decision or a sufficiently strong versioned revocation mechanism with defined failure behavior | Keep coalescing or caching only where it preserves the required permission-decision semantics

question: Traffic jumps faster than new servers can start. How would you protect the service while capacity catches up?
key_points: Protect scarce dependencies with bounded concurrency and explicit admission control | Prioritize essential work and shed or defer optional work where the product permits it | Use valid caching, precomputation or bounded asynchronous buffering for suitable requests | Reserve headroom and understand startup time rather than assuming autoscaling is instantaneous | Monitor backlog age, saturation and errors, then recover gradually without a retry surge | Keep overload behavior explicit so clients do not mistake acceptance for completion
common_misconceptions: Autoscaling always reacts before a short burst causes damage | An unbounded queue is a harmless way to accept every request | Retrying immediately at every layer reduces overload
probes: Which bottleneck might remain after more application servers start? | How would you decide that the queue is too old to keep accepting work? | What could trigger a second surge during recovery?
twist: Now excess requests are critical writes that must not be acknowledged before durable acceptance. What changes?
twist_key_points: Acknowledge only after the system has durably accepted the work under the required contract | Apply producer backpressure or a clear retryable failure before acceptance when durable capacity is exhausted | Do not silently drop accepted work or claim that an in-memory queue provides the required durability
